strengths: Provides the first rigorous characterization (to the authors' knowledge) of a fractal convergence boundary and chaotic dynamics (positive topological entropy, Li-Yorke chaos) for gradient descent in a genuinely high-dimensional, non-convex optimization setting (matrix factorization), going beyond prior univariate-loss chaos results (Kong and Tao, 2020; Chen et al., 2024b).

Derives an exact, tight critical step size for scalar factorization, improving on existing sufficient conditions (e.g., Wang et al., 2022), and precisely characterizes the convergence region up to measure zero.

Introduces an elegant quotient/semi-conjugacy technique (via the map T) that reduces the high-dimensional dynamics to a tractable 2D planar system, enabling rigorous analysis of self-similarity, invariant sets, and preimage structure (covering map / folding mechanism) that plausibly explains the chaos mechanism generally.

Extends theoretical results to general matrix factorization via an invariant subspace argument (covering identity initialization and residual networks), and supplements with experiments showing the qualitative phenomena (fractal boundary, sensitivity to initialization) persist under generic initializations and in deep matrix factorization, suggesting the theory captures a broader phenomenon.

Very thorough and mathematically careful appendix (60+ pages) with detailed proofs, connections to classical dynamical systems/fractal theory (Devaney chaos, Li-Yorke chaos, box-counting dimension), and honest discussion of how the setting differs from classical frameworks.
Clear, well-motivated framing (two central questions), good related-work positioning distinguishing from edge-of-stability/catapult literature and from prior finite-time chaos observations.
weaknesses: The rigorous results are confined to a fairly narrow setting: scalar factorization and matrix factorization restricted to a special orthogonal-initialization subspace W; general initializations and deep factorization are only explored empirically, with theory explicitly left as future work, limiting the generality of the main claims.

Practical significance is somewhat unclear: near-critical step sizes are rarely used in practice (they are typically associated with divergence or highly unstable training), so the direct relevance of these chaotic regimes to standard deep learning practice is not strongly established beyond qualitative analogy.

The paper's connection to real neural network training (nonlinear activations, SGD noise, minibatching) remains speculative; the bridge from linear/matrix factorization insights to broader implicit-bias or generalization phenomena in practical networks is not empirically or theoretically demonstrated.

The exposition is very dense and technical, with heavy reliance on appendix material for essentially all substantive proofs; the main text sometimes states strong claims (e.g., mechanism section) with proofs deferred/incomplete ('a rigorous investigation is left for future work'), which slightly weakens the completeness of the core narrative.

The distributional implicit bias phenomenon observed empirically (Figure 2 right) is intriguing but left unanalyzed, so the paper's own stated interesting finding is not theoretically supported, only demonstrated anecdotally.
Reproducibility statement/code link appears incomplete in the provided manuscript (empty link), though this may be an artifact of the provided PDF rather than the actual submission.

strengths: Provides the first rigorous characterization of chaos (positive topological entropy, Li-Yorke chaos, existence of periodic orbits of all periods) and fractal convergence-region geometry (self-similarity, box-counting dimension) for gradient descent in a genuinely multivariate/high-dimensional optimization setting, going beyond prior univariate-loss analyses (Kong and Tao, 2020; Chen et al., 2024b).

The exact critical step size derived in Theorem 1 strictly generalizes and improves upon the previous convergence condition of Wang et al. (2022), as explicitly demonstrated both analytically and visually (Figure 7).

The technical machinery (quotient dynamics via the map T, analysis of the multi-valued inverse of the planar map F, symbolic dynamics/conjugacy to piecewise-linear maps, covering-map argument for general polynomial networks) is original, carefully constructed, and the proofs in the appendix are thorough and mostly self-contained.

Results are extended from the simplified scalar factorization case to shallow matrix factorization with orthogonal/symmetric initialization subspaces, and a general (if weaker) covering-map property is shown for arbitrary polynomial neural networks, suggesting the mechanism (folding) is not an artifact of the toy setting.

Empirical validation extends convincingly beyond the theoretical regime: experiments on deep matrix factorization and ReLU networks trained on CIFAR-10 (Figures 4, 5, 9-13) show qualitatively persistent chaotic/fractal phenomena, strengthening the practical relevance of the theoretical claims.

The paper meaningfully challenges the common narrative that large-step-size GD has simple implicit biases (toward flatness, balance, or minimum norm), instead showing these quantities can take almost any admissible value depending sensitively on initialization — a conceptually important and well-supported finding.

Clear, well-organized structure with an extensive appendix that situates the work relative to classical chaos/fractal theory (Devaney chaos, Li-Yorke chaos, Wada basins, McDonald et al. classification) and explains precisely why classical tools do not directly apply.
weaknesses: The strongest, fully rigorous results (Theorems 1, 2, 4, 5) are confined to scalar (rank-1) factorization and to a very particular symmetric/orthogonal initialization subspace W for general matrix factorization; extension to fully general initializations or deep factorization is only demonstrated empirically (Appendix I), leaving a gap between the theory and the more general claims made in the abstract/intro.

Proposition 6 (covering map for general polynomial networks) is comparatively weak: it only asserts GD acts as a covering map outside a measure-zero set, without establishing that this leads to folding of an invariant boundary set, chaos, or fractality — the central phenomena of the paper are not actually proven in this general setting.

The practical significance of operating exactly at or near the critical step size is not strongly established; practitioners typically use step sizes well below the divergence threshold, and the paper's discussion of real-world relevance (Section 4.3) is largely qualitative/exploratory rather than quantitatively connected to typical training regimes or generalization outcomes.

The exposition is extremely dense and notation-heavy (many auxiliary maps T, F, Q, G_i, quotient dynamics, etc.), which may substantially limit accessibility even for a specialized theoretical ML audience; intuition for why chaos arises is given but could be foregrounded more in the main text before the heavy formalism.

No quantitative fractal-dimension or entropy estimates are provided for the deep/general matrix factorization or CIFAR-10 ReLU experiments, so the connection between the rigorously proven cases and the empirically observed fractal patterns in more general settings remains suggestive rather than quantified.

The reproducibility statement leaves the code link blank/missing in the manuscript, which is a minor completeness concern for a paper whose claims rely partly on numerically estimated quantities (e.g., box-counting dimension).

strengths: The paper provides rigorous, exact characterizations (critical step size, convergence region, self-similarity degree, topological entropy bounds) for gradient descent in scalar and shallow matrix factorization, going beyond prior asymptotic/threshold results (e.g., improving on Wang et al. 2022's sufficient conditions with a tight, almost-everywhere exact region).

The connection drawn between gradient descent update maps, covering-map/folding behavior, and classical dynamical-systems notions of chaos (topological entropy, Li-Yorke chaos, Devaney chaos, self-similar fractal boundaries, box-counting dimension) is conceptually interesting and, to the authors' claim, novel in the ML optimization literature.

The theoretical results are extended (with rigorous proofs) from the scalar case to general matrix factorization restricted to an orthogonal-initialization invariant subspace, covering commonly used initialization schemes (identity/scaled-identity, zero-asymmetric).

The appendix is unusually thorough: detailed proofs for every stated theorem/proposition, discussion relating the results to classical fractal-basin-boundary and chaos theory, and a careful comparison against the closest prior work (Wang et al., 2022).

Empirical experiments extend the toy-model insights qualitatively to more realistic settings: deep matrix factorization and depth-3 ReLU networks on CIFAR-10 subsets, showing similar fractal sensitivity-to-initialization and sharpness distributions, which strengthens the claim that the phenomenon is not purely an artifact of the simplified model.

The paper is well positioned relative to a large body of related work (Edge of Stability, catapult, implicit bias, chaos-in-optimization literature), with a clear articulation of what is new relative to each line.
weaknesses: The fully rigorous results are confined to very low-dimensional/simplified settings (scalar factorization, or matrix factorization restricted to a measure-zero orthogonal-initialization subspace W); the extension to general initializations and deep factorization/nonlinear networks is only empirical (Appendix I/J), so the central 'fractal chaos' claim for realistic settings is not proven, only illustrated on small, low-epoch, 2-class experiments.

Proposition 6, which is supposed to justify the general covering-map mechanism for arbitrary polynomial-activation networks, is quite weak: it only shows GD is a covering map on parameter space minus a measure-zero set, but explicitly does not establish that GD(C) ⊃ C or that C contains a basin boundary, which are the key ingredients actually driving the chaos/fractal phenomena described earlier in the paper. This leaves a fairly large gap between the toy-model theory and the claimed general mechanism.

The practical significance/impact of the results is not entirely clear: near-critical step sizes are a narrow and somewhat idiosyncratic regime (as opposed to the well-studied EoS regime with step sizes below 2/η_sharpness), and the paper does not discuss how often or why practitioners would operate near this exact critical boundary, nor what actionable implications (e.g., for hyperparameter selection or generalization) follow from the chaos characterization beyond the negative statement that 'no simple implicit bias exists.'

The empirical validation on real data is limited in scale (very small networks: 2 hidden layers with 25-100 neurons, 2-class 25-image subsets of CIFAR-10) and the fractal dimension estimates rely on numerical box-counting on 2D random slices, which is suggestive but not a rigorous proof of fractality in the higher-dimensional realistic setting.

The paper's exposition is extremely dense and notation-heavy (many auxiliary quotient maps T, F, Q, κ, multiple invariant sets Z, A0, A1, A2, B), which, combined with pushing nearly all technical content to a 40+ page appendix, makes the paper difficult to verify without substantial effort; the main text alone provides limited intuition for why the very intricate machinery (quotient dynamics, preimage structure, Lyapunov-like function Q) is necessary.

The reported box-counting dimension (1.249) and topological entropy lower bound (log 3) are somewhat narrow, model-specific quantities whose broader relevance to understanding neural network training dynamics beyond this factorization toy model remains speculative, and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this gap is left to future work.

strengths: Provides the first rigorous characterization of chaotic dynamics (positive topological entropy, Li-Yorke/Devaney chaos, periodic orbits of all periods) and fractal convergence boundaries for gradient descent in a concrete, well-motivated non-convex setting (matrix/scalar factorization), addressing a gap explicitly noted relative to prior work (Kong & Tao 2020; Chen et al. 2024b) that was restricted to univariate losses.

Derives an exact, tight critical step size for convergence in scalar-vector factorization (Theorem 1), improving on and provably generalizing prior partial results (e.g., Wang et al. 2022), with a clear quantitative comparison (Figure 7) demonstrating the tightness gain.

Elegant proof technique via an equivariance/quotient dynamical system (map T and the induced planar system F) that reduces a high-dimensional problem to a 2D dynamical system, enabling rigorous analysis of self-similarity, covering maps, and folding behavior; this machinery is reused effectively across multiple theorems.

Clearly identifies a general mechanism (covering-map/folding behavior of the GD update map) underlying the chaos and shows it extends, at least partially, to general polynomial neural networks (Proposition 6), giving the results some generality beyond the core matrix factorization setting.

Strong extension from the simplified scalar case to general matrix factorization with orthogonal initializations, and empirical validation showing the same qualitative fractal/chaotic phenomena persist under general (non-orthogonal) initializations, deep matrix factorization, and real ReLU networks trained on CIFAR-10 subsets.

The paper directly engages with and complicates the literature's narrative of simple implicit biases (balancedness, minimum norm, flatness) of large-step-size GD, showing empirically and theoretically that no such simple bias exists near the convergence boundary, which is a conceptually important and non-obvious message.

Very thorough appendix with complete, careful proofs, discussion of relation to classical fractal/chaos theory (quasicircles, Wada basins, Li-Yorke vs. Devaney chaos), and quantitative measures (topological entropy, box-counting dimension, uncertainty exponent) that connect the abstract theory to interpretable practical claims about unpredictability.
weaknesses: The rigorous theoretical results are essentially confined to scalar/vector factorization and matrix factorization restricted to a special orthogonal-initialization subspace W; the extension to fully general initializations, deep matrix factorization, and nonlinear neural networks is only supported empirically (Section 4.3, Appendix I/J), leaving a gap between the strong theory and the practically relevant settings.

Proposition 6, the only general result for broader neural networks, merely establishes that GD acts as a covering map almost everywhere outside a measure-zero set; it explicitly does not establish whether the folding set C is invariant or contains a basin boundary, so it does not by itself imply chaos or fractal boundaries in general networks — the link to Section 4.3's neural net experiments is suggestive rather than proven.

The real-data experiments (Section 4.3, Appendix J) use very small-scale settings (2-hidden-layer networks with 25–100 neurons, 25 images, 2-class CIFAR-10 subsets), which is reasonable for illustrating qualitative phenomena but limits the strength of claims about relevance to realistic deep learning training regimes.

The paper's practical takeaways for practitioners are limited: the main message is that near-critical step sizes are chaotic and unpredictable, but there is little guidance on how to detect or avoid this regime in practice beyond noting its existence, and the 'future directions' section frames much of the follow-up (distributional implicit bias) as open.
The reproducibility statement leaves the code link blank/unspecified in the provided version, so reproducibility could not be fully verified from the manuscript alone.

Some of the proofs rely on delicate case-by-case algebraic analysis (e.g., Appendix E, G) which, while apparently correct, makes the paper very dense and could benefit from more intuition/visual summary of proof strategy in the main text for readers who are not dynamical-systems specialists.
